blocks.text: Ninety seconds after the Loose, three Cold Fleet birds had already gone downwind like thrown slates, skating out over the reed toward the sluice and never once looking back for the others. The reed lay down flat and silver under the gale all the way to the sluice gates, combed in one direction like the coat of an animal stroked from the head, and the light under the cloud was low and yellow, the colour of lamp oil. It gave me about twenty-eight minutes before roost-light.
Wenlode's Tackers stood a pace off Joan and Mercy, exactly where the flight book had said they would stand. Above us my herding shades were being torn from the flock's edge one by one.

I had raised all six at the Loose along the flock's upwind side, the way every Wing is taught, to lean on it a little. It did not lean. Cold Fleet in a gale is less a flock than a weather of its own: it went up off the crate in one dark breath and the wind took it whole and threw it down the Reedbed, and my shades, which can fly no faster than the runners beneath them, were left behind it in the air like gloves dropped on a road. Each time one of them dropped out of the flock's reach, a bird somewhere at the edge let go of it and was only a bird among birds again, and I felt the thread go slack the way a line goes slack in your hand.
Wenlode's Wing, a lean grey man in a sluice-keeper's oilskin, had his shades at my ceiling, shade on shade. He hardly needed to. The wind was doing his work for him.
We had been ringed at half past three in the Sluice House, a stone room at the foot of the hill with the river roaring through the gates on the other side of the wall.

Joan took the withy first. She had never worn one. I held the plaited reed out to her on my open hand, and she took it from my hand onto her own wrist, and to steady herself she put her other hand on my wrist while she did it. Her fingers were very cold. I closed her ring next, twenty-three, as gently as my numb fingers would let me, turning her wrist in my hand to find the place where the copper would sit without pinching, because she was giving me something she was afraid of and I wanted what I gave her back to be comfortable. Then Mercy, twenty-four; Abel, twenty-five; Rhys, twenty-six; Lucas, twenty-seven; my own seventy-one last, one-handed, and my hands did not shake this time.

One of the four counters was Dorcas Ely, who had written forty on our sheet at Hobsmere. She wrote our six numbers down the margin of the team sheet in a small upright hand and did not look at me. The eldest counter asked whether any player was sighted and wished to declare it. Nobody spoke. Lucas looked at his hands.

Then the counters drew ends. The eldest put his hand in the felt bag and brought out the brass token and read it: Hobsmere to attack the south-west Roost. The gale was coming off the sea out of the north-east. We had the downwind end.
"There," Rhys said. "The Fen's leaning our way for once, Crate. I knew it would come to its senses about me."
"It isn't a gift," I said. "Cold Fleet won't stop at a Roost mouth in this. It'll go straight past and come apart."
"And what does a home side want on a day like this, Rhys?" Joan said. "Nothing settled and a point each, isn't it? They'll keep it loose and let the wind do their defending."
At nine minutes to four, six call-minutes in, I dropped all six shades.
I gave Joan the open hand and she passed it to Mercy. Then I stopped trying to move the flock and only looked at it, which costs nothing, and which I should have done from the Loose.

The gale had pinned the grain. Every few minutes the flock clawed its way back up the field, low, in the lee of the sluice wall where the wind broke, a long dark ribbon pouring along the stone; and then it rose out of the lee, and the gale caught it and flung it down the length of the Reedbed toward the south-west Roost, and past it, and out over the reed beyond. Twice I watched the Wenlode Wing lean his shades on the flock's downwind edge to hold it up the field, away from his Roost, and twice the birds he leaned on were shrugged: their neighbours stopped counting them, and they dropped out of the flock's notice and fell to its edge like leaves off a gate, and his shades on them were wasted. Upwind was against the grain. The only thing Cold Fleet would do today was run before the wind, and if nothing held it, it would run past any Roost on the Fen.

So I read threads. I found the point bird on the next downwind run, the bird at the leading edge with the gale at its back, and followed the seven bright threads from it to the seven birds it watched, and from each of those to theirs, as far as I can hold, which is about seven birds and no further. At eight minutes past four, with the flock clawing back along the wall, I raised my own shade alone, seventy-one, and set my ceiling at the height the point birds flew on their downwind runs. The Wenlode Wing matched me within the breath.
On the next run the flock came over my shade, and I read the point bird again, and I saw it.

It was not at the north-east edge. At every flight I had watched it had kept to the north-east edge, leaning on the flock, the way it had leaned on the Mallow birds at Hobsmere. Now it flew at my shade's wingtip, so close that their wings would have touched if either of them had been a bird, the old dull copper on its leg turned toward me. I followed the point bird's threads and counted them, because counting birds is my work: seven threads, seven neighbours, and the extra bird was the eighth nearest, just outside them. Close enough to be counted. A wingbeat nearer and it would have been one of the seven. It did not come the wingbeat nearer. It held itself there, at the edge of being counted, choosing not to be. I stood in the flattened reed with the gale pressing my coat against the backs of my legs and the light going yellow to brown over the sluice and the river shouting through the gates behind the wall, and I looked at it for longer than I should have, and I understood that it had come to that place on purpose, and that the place was beside me.

At a quarter past four the counters declared roost-light. The eldest called the counted flock in a voice the wind tore in half. The three birds that went downwind at the Loose had gone home to the Loft roof and the loft-men had them, and they were struck.
"Thirty-seven," Joan said at my shoulder, fierce and quiet. "Every one of them in, or it's two at best, isn't it?"
"Every one," I said.

The flight book had told us one more thing about Wenlode, and Joan had found it in the counters' notes and underlined it twice in pencil: at roost-light, every match, they sent the Tacker off the second Caller upwind with their decoys. He went now. He took the two wooden starlings on their poles and ran up the field into the wind, bent nearly double, to plant them by our Roost, and that left Mercy free and one marker on the field, and he was on Joan.

Rhys and Abel ran our decoys down to the south-west Roost and set them low by the mouth. Lucas was there already; the Reed's place is at the other side's Roost. I raised the five, Joan's first, and lowered my ceiling until my shades flew just above the thatch, and I felt the Wenlode Wing follow me down, as he had followed me all afternoon. For the length of a breath both our sets of shades lagged and smeared and then settled, at the same height, over the Roost mouth.

Mercy came in. I came in, running with the wind at my back so that I could hardly stop. And then Joan, last, not running, walking down the field with her hands in her pockets as if she were going to see about a blocked drain, and the Wenlode boy who had marked her all afternoon walked after her, a pace off, because that was what he had done in every match this season and the counters had written it down every time. She walked into the middle of us and stopped. He stopped a pace off her shoulder. His shade stopped over him, at my height, a hand's breadth from hers.
The flock came down the field.

I found the point bird as it came over the cluster, and I followed its threads, and there were seven, and every one of them ran to a shade. Abel's, Rhys's, Mercy's, Lucas's, mine, Joan's; and the seventh, short and bright, to the shade over the Wenlode boy. No real bird was nearer. For the length of a breath there were seven shades on the point bird and nothing else in all its world, and it was held. I felt it go still in the threads, the way a bird goes still in your hands when it stops struggling. Beside my shade, eighth nearest, the extra bird hung in the wind and did not come in.

The point bird went down. It went down with the gale behind it, into the lee of the thatch where the wind could not reach, and it took its seven with it, and they took theirs. I watched the threads draw tight from bird to bird back through the whole flock like a net being hauled. Cold Fleet folded in behind its point bird and poured into Wenlode's Roost, a dark stream of birds going in at the mouth, all of them, with no gap and no straggler, and the loft-men dropped the door.
The counters went to the Roost and counted through the wire, two and then the other two, and the eldest raised both flags.
"Thirty-seven in," he called. "Full settle. Hobsmere Cutters, four."
It was twenty-one minutes past four. Nineteen call-minutes, and no Breath owed, because my second call had run only thirteen.

The Wenlode boy stood looking at his Wing, and his Wing stood in the flattened reed with his oilskin cracking round him and looked at nothing at all. Behind me Rhys made a sound I had never heard a person make, and lifted Abel off the ground.

The counters cut our rings at the reed-line, Dorcas Ely's snips cold against my wrist. The withy stayed on Joan. When my shade was gone I looked up out of habit to the place where it had flown, and something was there still, a bird-shape at my old ceiling against the brown cloud, keeping above me. I thought it was what the clerk at the Ringing House had called it: an after-image, the sighted eye remembering. I was tired, and the pull was beginning, and I let myself believe him.

The loft-men crated Cold Fleet at the Roost and put the crates on a handcart and took them up the hill to the Circuit Loft, a few hundred yards, where they lived. When the handcart moved, my line moved with it.
"Nine," Joan said, and took my hand. "Nineteen called, ten free, nine to walk. That's the sum, isn't it?"

It was uphill. It ran away from the river and the sluice and every piece of water in Wenlode, straight up the cobbles toward the Loft, and I felt Joan understand that through my hand, and her grip, which had been hard, went a little easier.
"Uphill," she said. "Away from the water. First kind thing this county's done for us in a month."

She talked the whole way. She told me how a sluice works, how the gates are wound up on a rack and the river let through by the inch. She swore at the Wenlode drainage board, at the man who had laid the cobbles, at the gale. Lucas walked behind us with his watch in his hand and called the minutes, quietly, in his precise voice, and once when I looked back he was not looking at me but above my head, and then he looked at the cobbles.

The pull was worst at the Loft gate. I had come through that gate every morning for three winters with a pail in each hand, and through the wall I could hear Cold Fleet being put up on their perches, the soft high bickering I knew better than most voices, and every part of me that was not holding Joan's hand wanted to go in and stand among them in the dark. Joan did not stop. She did not let go. She walked me past the gate and on up the hill toward the Ringing House, swearing about back-flow in a low steady voice, and Lucas behind us said, "Seven," and then, "Eight," and then, "Nine," and the line in my chest went slack and lay down like the reed.
Full dark came while we stood there. I did not see the shape above me leave. I only noticed, after, that I could not see it.

At Wenlode the counters write up the sheet in the front office of the Circuit Loft, and both Wings sign it. The Wenlode Wing signed under me in a large slow hand and then shook my hand, and his was as cold as mine.

"Well flown, Miss Tansley," he said. "I'll not say otherwise. You'll not do it twice, mind." He was not unkind; he said it the way you tell someone the bridge is out further down. "The cure's simple, once a body thinks of it. Any shade of mine gets pulled into your cluster, I drop it. Then you've six, and six won't hold." He buttoned his oilskin. "I'll be thinking of it all the way home."
"Thank you," I said, and meant it, because he was right, and he had not had to tell me.
Dorcas Ely wrote our six numbers against the settle, twenty-three to twenty-seven and seventy-one, and one Wenlode number beside them. She still did not look at me.
The yard was dark when we came out, the lamps lit in the loft windows and the weathercock still swinging. Rhys and Abel and Mercy had gone down to the van. Lucas had waited by the gate.
"I need to tell you both something," he said. "I'd rather do it here than anywhere I'll have to go back to."
Joan looked at him, and then at me, and said nothing, which is not like her.

"I'm sighted," Lucas said. "I always have been. I've never declared it. I didn't at Hobsmere, and I didn't today." He held his scarred hand in his other hand, the way you hold a part you are afraid of dropping. "At the Gadwell match, in the Gloaming, I saw the extra bird come down out of the flock at Hamish's shade. It dived at it, the w-way a hawk dives. And I felt it here." He touched his chest. "It's like an escapement when the pallet slips. The whole train runs at once and you can't catch it. On the shore, when Hamish pulled toward the w-water, I was pulled with him. That's what happens to a sighted tether. I knew the rule. I took the withy anyway, because nobody else would." He stopped. "That's why I let go. Of him, and of you, at minute nine. I wasn't afraid of the water. I was going into it."
"Thank you for telling me," I said. "You came back at first light. You walked me down and your hand didn't shake."
"I looked at your hands," he said. "Only at your hands. I didn't look at the mere once."
"I know. I was there."

Joan had been looking at the dark beyond the yard for so long that I thought she was angry, and then I saw her face in the lamp from the loft window and it was not anger. It was something older, and it was not about Lucas at all.
"Well," she said at last. "That's said, and it stays in this yard, doesn't it." It was not a question. "Nobody else needs the trouble of it."
Lucas nodded. I took his scarred hand and held it for a moment, the way I would hold a bird that had flown into a window, and then I let it go.

On Sunday I took the train out to the sanatorium on its rise among the pines, alone. Hamish was in a chair by the window with a rug over his knees, thinner than when I had seen him last, his breath catching at the top of every breath. He had read the result in the Courier. The paper was folded on the sill at the page.
"Four," he said. "At Wenlode. In that."

I told him how. I told him plainly, the gale and the shrugged birds and the threads and the Wenlode boy walking in after Joan, the seven shades on the point bird and the flock going down into the lee of the thatch. He listened with his eyes shut. When I had finished he asked, without opening them, "And it?"
"It was at my shade's wingtip," I said. "All match. Eighth nearest to the point bird. It could have been one of the seven, and it stayed just outside."

For a long time he did not say anything. Out in the pines a mistle thrush was singing into the last of the wind, a loud wild broken song, the song of a bird that sings in storms, and the light lay grey and level along the sill.

"It came for mine," Hamish said. "Against Gadwell. In the Gloaming. It came down out of the flock at my shade, the way a hawk comes. And I heard it. Not with my ears." He opened his eyes and looked at me. "One word. Just the one. 'Not you.'"

The thrush stopped. I sat very still in the hard chair with my hands in my lap, and I looked out past him at the pines moving and the grey sky moving behind them and the long fen beyond, all the way to the rim of the world, and I went back through the whole of Saturday as carefully as I have ever gone through anything, bird by bird and minute by minute, and I came to the place at the reed-line where I had looked up at the brown cloud with my ring already cut and no shade left in the sky at all, and to Lucas on the cobbles, looking above my head.

It had not been an after-image. It had spent the whole match at my wingtip, and after the door dropped and my shades came down it had not gone back to the flock; it had stayed above me, at my old ceiling, all the way up the hill, over me and not over the birds, until full dark.
